blurb: The solid-red sport of Minnesota's 'Haralson': firm, crisp, juicy, tart flesh and a 3–5-month keeper, a shade earlier and redder than its parent. Hits the tart-crisp brief — a workmanlike crisp rather than a Honeycrisp explosion.
size: ~12–15 ft × 12–15 ft on semi-dwarf rootstock (a naturally smallish, spreading tree; 20+ ft standard)
water: Moderate, regular — deep weekly soak in summer
spread: Clumping — single grafted tree; needs a pollinizer apple other than Haralson
seasons: Pink-budded white blossom mid-spring; solid-red fruit late Sept–early Oct
wildlife: Blossoms feed bees; dropped fruit feeds birds & mammals
toxic: Fruit flesh edible; seeds contain cyanogenic amygdalin (mildly toxic if chewed in quantity)
origin: Central Asia and Afghanistan; sport found in La Crescent, Minnesota
habitat: Wild fruit-tree forests and mountain slopes of Central Asia

care.hardiness: 'Haralred' is a solid-red bud-sport of 'Haralson', the University of Minnesota's 1922 all-purpose apple (Malinda open-pollinated); the red limb was found by orchardist Louis Lautz of La Crescent, Minnesota, and Bailey Nurseries introduced it, rating it USDA zones 3–7.[6][12] It inherits Haralson's iron constitution — the parent is approved for every Minnesota fruit zone and rated hardy through zones 3–5 in Wisconsin's cultivar guide — and University of Idaho lists 'Haralred' itself among apples adapted to cold, short-season areas, while University of Wyoming Extension names it among the varieties known to thrive in Wyoming, a climate much like the Front Range's.[6][7][8][9] Boulder's 5b–6a winters are therefore no concern at all; the local risk is a late spring frost on the open bloom, which is a siting problem, not a hardiness one.[1][2]
care.planting: Plant in spring once the ground is workable (April–May), or in early fall, in full sun on a high spot so cold air drains past rather than pooling around the buds — avoid frost-pocket lows and the warm south or west wall of a building, which pushes bloom too early into frost danger.[1][2] Bare-root trees go in while dormant; container stock anytime in the growing season. In a pot the roots are far less cold-hardy than the canopy and freeze far harder than ground roots over a Front Range winter, so a containerized apple needs a large (≥20 gal) pot, a sheltered or heeled-in spot out of desiccating wind, and a move to an unheated garage in a hard cold snap; plan to plant it in the ground within a year or two.[3]
care.sun: Full sun — at least 6 hours of direct sun, and the more the better for fruit set, sugar, and the deep red finish that is the whole point of this sport over striped Haralson.[1][4] Shade cuts cropping and invites disease.[4]
care.soil: Tolerates a wide range of soils, including Boulder's alkaline (>8.0) clay-loam, and does best in well-drained ground near neutral 6.0–7.0.[4] Amend heavy clay with organic matter at planting to speed establishment and improve drainage; never plant where water stands.[1]
care.water: Moderate but regular — a deep weekly soak through the dry Front Range summer keeps the fruit sizing and the tree stress-free, especially the first few years while roots establish. Water at the dripline, not the trunk, and avoid chronic wet feet, which invites root rot.[1][3]
care.spacing: Size depends on rootstock: dwarf trees want about 6–8 ft, semi-dwarf 12–15 ft, and standard (seedling) trees 20–25 ft apart.[3] Haralson-type trees are naturally on the small, spreading side for an apple — the parent is described as hardy and vigorous but relatively small — so a semi-dwarf 'Haralred' makes a manageable 12–15 ft backyard tree with room left for the second variety it needs.[6][7]
care.propagation: Apples do not come true from seed, and a sport is a limb mutation, so 'Haralred' exists only as grafted or budded wood traced back to the red-fruited Lautz limb — never grow it from its own pips, which would give a random seedling.[4][12] The rootstock sets mature size and how soon the tree bears (dwarf, semi-dwarf, or standard), so buy a grafted tree on a rootstock matched to your space.[3][4]
care.bloom: Pink-budded white blossom opens in mid-spring, typically May on the Front Range, in the same window as its parent.[1][4] Apples need pollen from a different, co-blooming variety, and here is the trap with this one: a sport is genetically the same apple as its parent, so 'Haralred' and 'Haralson' cannot pollinate each other — the introducer states plainly that it is an unsuitable pollinator for Haralson.[2][12] Plant a third, different apple or a flowering crabapple within about 100 ft whose bloom overlaps.[2][3]
care.feeding: Feed lightly. A modest spring application of a balanced fertilizer supports young trees, but avoid heavy nitrogen — lush, soft growth both delays fruiting and dramatically increases fire-blight susceptibility, a real hazard in warm, moist Front Range springs.[1][3]
care.pruning: Do the main structural pruning while fully dormant in late winter (February into early March here). Haralson-type trees build a strongly developed central leader with wide-angled lateral branches almost on their own, so training is mostly a matter of keeping one leader, spacing the scaffold tiers, and thinning crossing, crowded, and inward wood to let light and air into the canopy.[1][3][6] Fire blight is the Front Range risk: it spreads on tools and through fresh cuts in warm, wet weather, so never prune during active growth or wet spells, disinfect pruners between cuts (10% bleach or 70% alcohol), and cut any strike out 8–12 in below the visibly dead tissue in dry weather — the cultivar's fire-blight resistance is real but moderate, not immunity.[1][3][7][8]
care.maintenance: Thin the fruit. Haralson sets in clusters and tends toward biennial bearing, and North Dakota's Carrington trial found its 'Haralred' bearing precociously every year on every branch — their note is simply 'Thin the fruit!' — so in late June or early July reduce clusters to one or two apples, 4–6 in apart along the branch, for size and a crop every year.[3][6][10]
care.troubles: Disease-wise this is a solid, not bulletproof, apple: the parent is only slightly susceptible to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, and Wisconsin rates it moderately resistant to both, while Idaho lists fire-blight resistance for 'Haralred' itself; the weak spot is apple scab, to which Haralson is moderately susceptible — though Colorado's dry climate usually limits fungal disease outside extended wet spells.[1][6][7][8] Keep nitrogen modest and cut fire-blight strikes out 8–12 in below the dead tissue in dry weather, sterilizing pruners between cuts.[1][3] Codling moth (the wormy-apple pest) is the most serious fruit pest here and needs monitoring and timed control for clean fruit; cleaning up dropped fruit and leaves each fall helps.[1][2] One honest caveat from the far north: at NDSU's Carrington station (a shorter, cooler season than Boulder's) 'Haralred' ripened very late with weak flavor and the reviewers concluded there were better choices, even as home growers reported fine fruit — so give it the sunniest spot you have and let it hang to full color.[10][11]
care.harvest: Pick late September into early October on the Front Range — Idaho lists a late-September harvest for 'Haralred', and Haralson comes off around October 1 in Wisconsin and late September to early October in Minnesota; the sport colors up a solid red and runs a little earlier than its red-striped parent.[3][7][8][12] How it eats: the flesh is white, firm, crisp, and juicy — Minnesota's own description calls it medium-tender crisp, mildly acid, while Wisconsin's guide rates it crisp, juicy, and tart with a distinctive flavor — so expect a clean tart-crisp apple, a workmanlike crunch rather than Honeycrisp's shatter.[6][7] It is a genuine keeper: the introducer calls it juicy, tart, firm and a good keeper, and the parent stores about 3 months in Wisconsin's rating and 4–5 months in Minnesota's, staying firm rather than going mealy; its tartness mellows a little in storage and it makes an excellent pie and sauce apple.[3][6][7][12]
care.companions: Plant a different apple variety or a compatible flowering crabapple within ~100 ft as the essential pollinizer — and not Haralson, which this sport cannot cross-pollinate.[2][3][12] Keep the root zone in low groundcover or mulch rather than competing turf, and site away from junipers and hawthorns that share apple diseases (cedar-apple rust, fire blight).[1]

edible.card: Crisp, tart, juicy fruit — fresh, pie, sauce, or cider
edible.summary: The fruit is a firm, crisp, juicy, tart all-purpose apple — fresh eating for those who like a sharp apple, and a classic pie and sauce apple that keeps 3–5 months; only the seeds carry a trace toxin.[3][6][7][5]
edible.parts: The fruit (flesh and skin) is the edible part, fresh or cooked.[4] 'Haralred' is Haralson in a red skin: white, firm flesh that is crisp and juicy, medium-tender rather than rock-hard, with a mildly acid to distinctly tart flavor — good for pie, sauce, freezing, fresh eating, and baking — and it is a reliable keeper that stays firm for several months in cold storage instead of softening or going mealy.[6][7][12]
edible.preparation: Eat fresh out of hand (the tartness mellows after some weeks in storage), or core and slice for pies, crisps, sauce, freezing, drying, and juice or cider.[3][6] Cut out and discard the seedy core — the flesh needs no special preparation to be safe.[5]
edible.caution: The flesh and skin are entirely safe; the only concern is the seeds, which (like all apples and stone fruit) contain cyanogenic amygdalin. Amygdalin releases hydrogen cyanide only when seeds are crushed or chewed — whole seeds swallowed by accident pass through harmlessly, and a person would have to deliberately chew on the order of dozens to hundreds of seeds to risk poisoning — so simply core the apple and don't eat or grind the pips, and keep children and pets from chewing them.[5]
